(a) In General.—There is established the Rio Grande Natural Area in the State of Colorado to conserve, restore, and protect the natural, historic, cultural, scientific, scenic, wildlife, and recreational resources of the Natural Area.  
    (b) Boundaries.—The Natural Area shall include the Rio Grande River from the southern boundary of the Alamosa National Wildlife Refuge to the New Mexico State border, extending ¼ mile on either side of the bank of the River.  
    (c) Map and Legal Description.—
        (1) In general.—As soon as practicable after the date of enactment of this Act, the Secretary shall prepare a map and legal description of the Natural Area.  
        (2) Effect.—The map and legal description of the Natural Area shall have the same force and effect as if included in this Act, except that the Secretary may correct any minor errors in the map and legal description.  
        (3) Public availability.—The map and legal description of the Natural Area shall be available for public inspection in the appropriate offices of the Bureau of Land Management.

fable.w: The tempting reading is that "public inspection" of the map signals public involvement, but this only makes a finished document available for viewing and gives outsiders no way to comment on, be consulted about, or challenge a federal decision. The section establishes the Natural Area, sets its boundaries, and directs the Secretary to prepare a map, with no advisory body, hearing, rulemaking, or consultation with states, tribes, or the public.
fable.s: The map and legal description of the Natural Area shall be available for public inspection in the appropriate offices of the Bureau of Land Management.

opus.w: The section creates the Natural Area, sets its boundaries, and has the Secretary prepare a map, with power to fix minor errors, without consulting anyone outside the federal government. Making the map available for public inspection only shares a finished product. It gives outsiders no role in a federal decision: no comment, hearing, consultation, advisory input or right to sue. So it is not participation.
opus.s: The map and legal description of the Natural Area shall be available for public inspection in the appropriate offices of the Bureau of Land Management.
opus.b:
1. **Tempting reading.** Subsection (c)(3) makes the map and legal description "available for public inspection," which can look like it brings the public into the process. It doesn't meet the definition. Public inspection only lets people see a finished document. There is no comment period, hearing, consultation, advisory body or right to sue. The Secretary prepares and corrects the map alone.

qwen_chat.w: The section requires the Secretary to prepare a map and make it available for public inspection. This is a transparency measure, not a participation mechanism. The definition of participation requires consultation, coordination, or formal involvement of outside parties in the decision-making process (e.g., advisory boards, comment periods, hearings). Merely allowing the public to view a document after it has been prepared does not constitute participation in the decision.
qwen_chat.s: (3) Public availability.—The map and legal description of the Natural Area shall be available for public inspection in the appropriate offices of the Bureau of Land Management.
qwen_chat.b: Tempting-but-wrong reading: One might argue that making the map "available for public inspection" constitutes participation because the public can see the decision. However, the definition requires that the government *consult* or *coordinate* with outsiders *before* making a decision, or that outsiders have a formal role (like an advisory board or right to sue). Mere availability of information for inspection is passive and does not involve the public in the decision-making process itself. The Secretary prepares the map unilaterally; there is no requirement for public comment, hearing, or consultation before the map is finalized.
